title: Tip the Crate Clockwise
statement:
A crate seen from the side is an m × n grid crate of single characters:

  • "#" is a loose stone,
  • "*" is a fixed obstacle,
  • "." is empty space.

Tip the crate 90° clockwise onto its side. Gravity then pulls every stone straight down until it rests on an obstacle, on another stone, or on the floor. Obstacles never move, and gravity does not change how the crate turned.

Return the grid after tipping, which has n rows and m columns.

examples.why: The single row becomes a column. Both stones fall to the bottom of it.
After the turn, the old bottom row becomes the left column and its stone falls to the floor. The top-left stone sits on the obstacle and cannot move.
The obstacle splits the column. The stones above it stay above it; only the one below drops to the floor.

hints: Turning clockwise makes each row a column, and its right end becomes the bottom. So you can let stones slide to the right inside each row first, then rotate.
Within a row, obstacles split it into separate stretches. In each stretch, the stones pile up against its right end.

Scan each row from right to left with a pointer to the next free slot. A stone moves to that slot and the slot moves left; an obstacle resets the slot to just left of itself. Then write cell (i, j) to (j, m − 1 − i).

explain.intuition:
Do the two effects in whichever order is easiest. After a clockwise turn, the right end of each row ends up at the bottom, so "falling down" afterwards is the same as "sliding right" before. Each row is then its own small problem.

Within a row, scan from the right with a write pointer free, the lowest empty slot a stone could drop into. A stone moves to free and free steps left. An obstacle is a new floor: free jumps to just left of it. That is one pass per row, like compacting an array in place. The rotation itself is pure index mapping: cell (i, j) goes to row j, column m − 1 − i.
steps: For each row i, set free = n − 1 and scan j from n − 1 down to 0.
If the cell is "*", set free = j − 1.
If the cell is "#", clear it to ".", put "#" at free, and decrement free.
Create an n × m result and set result[j][m − 1 − i] = row i, cell j.
pitfalls: Rotating the wrong way: result[j][i] is a transpose, and result[n − 1 − j][i] is counter-clockwise.
Letting stones fall past an obstacle. Each obstacle starts a new stretch.
Writing the stone before clearing its old cell, which erases it when the stone does not move (free == j).

solutions.title: Move stones one step at a time
solutions.idea: Repeatedly move any stone that has empty space to its right, until nothing moves. Then rotate.

solutions.title: Write pointer per row, then rotate
solutions.idea: Scan each row from the right, dropping each stone into the lowest free slot; an obstacle resets the slot. Then map (i, j) to (j, m − 1 − i).

followups: Tip it counter-clockwise instead. Which way do stones slide before the turn, and how does the index mapping change?
Count the stones that end up resting on an obstacle, without building the rotated grid.
